Appendix K Proof of the Interval Translation Lemma

Lemma K.1 (Restatement of Lemma 4.4).

Let N=2nN=2^{n} and fix r∈{0,…,N−1}r\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}. For an interval I=[α,β)⊆[0,N)I=[\alpha,\beta)\subseteq[0,N) and the map x^=(x+r)modN\hat{x}=(x+r)\bmod N, the image Tr​(I)T_{r}(I) is the cyclic interval [α+r,β+r)modN[\alpha+r,\beta+r)\bmod N, which is either a single standard interval or a union of two standard intervals. Across a full partition 0=α0<⋯<αm=N0=\alpha_{0}<\cdots<\alpha_{m}=N, at most one interval splits after translation.

Proof.

The map TrT_{r} is a rotation on the circle ℤN\mathbb{Z}_{N}. The image of I=[α,β)I=[\alpha,\beta) is

Tr​(I)\displaystyle T_{r}(I) ={(x+r)modN:x∈[α,β)}\displaystyle=\{(x+r)\bmod N:x\in[\alpha,\beta)\}
=[α+r,β+r)modN.\displaystyle=[\alpha+r,\beta+r)\bmod N.

Write a:=α+ra:=\alpha+r and b:=β+rb:=\beta+r (so 0≤a<b<2​N0\leq a<b<2N). There are three cases: (i) if b≤Nb\leq N, then Tr​(I)=[a,b)T_{r}(I)=[a,b) is a standard interval; (ii) if a≥Na\geq N, then both endpoints wrap and Tr(I)=[a−N,b−N)T_{r}(I)=[a-N,b-N) is a standard interval; (iii) if a<N<ba<N<b, then the image wraps around NN and Tr(I)=[a,N)∪[0,b−N)T_{r}(I)=[a,N)\cup[0,b-N), a union of two standard intervals.

For a full partition, the only way an interval splits is if the wrap point x0:=(N−r)modN∈[0,N)x_{0}:=(N-r)\bmod N\in[0,N) lies strictly inside that interval in xx-space (equivalently, if 00 lies strictly inside its image in x^\hat{x}-space). Since x0x_{0} is a single point and the intervals are disjoint, at most one interval contains it, hence at most one interval splits (and if x0x_{0} hits a boundary, no interval splits). ∎

Appendix L Correctness of Compilation and the Two-Call Theorem

This section provides a full proof of Theorem 4.6. We first formalize the compiled evaluation procedure and then prove correctness and the stated complexity bound.

L.1 Compiled Gate Evaluation Procedure

Fix a typed operator specification F:𝖠n→𝖠nr×𝖡ℓF:\mathsf{A}_{n}\to\mathsf{A}_{n}^{r}\times\mathsf{B}^{\ell} with partition (αi)i=0m(\alpha_{i})_{i=0}^{m} and per-interval data (Pi,Bi)(P_{i},B_{i}). Fix preprocessing mask rin∈Rr_{\mathrm{in}}\in R and define x^=x+rinmod2n\hat{x}=x+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bmod 2^{n}.

The compiler emits: (i) a predicate primitive instance Πpred\Pi_{\mathrm{pred}} producing XOR-shares of all primitive masked comparisons required by the rewritten Boolean circuit, and (ii) an interval-lookup primitive instance Πcoeff\Pi_{\mathrm{coeff}} producing additive shares of the active interval’s coefficient vector and auxiliary constants.

Online evaluation on a shared input ⟦x⟧\llbracket x\rrbracket proceeds as:

  1. 1.

    Materialize public x^\hat{x} by opening x^=x+rin\hat{x}=x+r_{\mathrm{in}} (Protocol 1).

  2. 2.

    Run Πpred\Pi_{\mathrm{pred}} (if needed) to obtain XOR-shares of all required primitive masked comparisons on x^\hat{x} and its public views (low bits, shifts).

  3. 3.

    Run Πcoeff\Pi_{\mathrm{coeff}} (if needed) to obtain additive shares of the active interval’s coefficient vector (and auxiliary constants).

  4. 4.

    Compute shares of x=x^−rinx=\hat{x}-r_{\mathrm{in}} locally (Protocol 2).

  5. 5.

    Evaluate rr degree-≤d\leq d polynomials via Horner’s rule using Beaver triples to obtain ⟦𝐲⟧∈Rr\llbracket\mathbf{y}\rrbracket\in R^{r}.

  6. 6.

    Evaluate the normalized Boolean circuit (Lemma D.2) over XOR shares using AND correlation to obtain ⟨𝐳⟩∈𝖡ℓ\langle\mathbf{z}\rangle\in\mathsf{B}^{\ell}, and apply any deterministic post-processing Φ\Phi using B2A/A2B as needed.

L.2 Proof of Theorem 4.6

Theorem L.1 (Restatement of Theorem 4.6).

Assume a backend provides: (i) a multi-view packed predicate primitive (Definition I.1), and (ii) an interval lookup primitive with vector payload. Then any scalar gate instance can be evaluated from a public masked input x^\hat{x} using at most two non-interactive backend interface evaluations, plus O⁡(r⋅d)O(r\cdot d) ring multiplications for Horner evaluation and the Boolean/mixed-domain costs stated in Theorem 4.6.

Proof.

We prove correctness and then the complexity bound.

Step 1: Correct Interval-Dependent Coefficient Selection.

Let the secret input be x∈Rx\in R with canonical representative in [0,2n)[0,2^{n}). Let i⋆i^{\star} be the unique index such that x∈Ii⋆=[αi⋆,αi⋆+1)x\in I_{i^{\star}}=[\alpha_{i^{\star}},\alpha_{i^{\star}+1}). By Lemma 4.4, the translated image of Ii⋆I_{i^{\star}} under x^=x+rinmod2n\hat{x}=x+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bmod 2^{n} is either: (i) one standard interval in x^\hat{x}-space, or (ii) two standard intervals when wrapping occurs. In compilation, if splitting occurs, the payload for the split interval is duplicated. Therefore, for the unique translated interval containing x^\hat{x}, the interval-lookup primitive returns additive shares of exactly the coefficient vector associated with Ii⋆I_{i^{\star}}.

Step 2: Correct Predicate Values Under Masking.

Consider any primitive predicate appearing in the predicate grammar.

  • •

    For unsigned comparisons Cβ(x)=𝕀[x<β]C_{\beta}(x)=\mathbb{I}_{\left[x<\beta\right]}, Lemma 4.3 expresses Cβ​(x)C_{\beta}(x) as an XOR of two masked comparisons on x^\hat{x} and a carry bit ww that depends only on the preprocessing mask and constants.

  • •

    For low-bit predicates Dγ,f(x)=𝕀[(xmod2f)<γ]D_{\gamma,f}(x)=\mathbb{I}_{\left[(x\bmod 2^{f})<\gamma\right]}, Lemma E.1 gives the analogous rewrite over ℤ2f\mathbb{Z}_{2^{f}}.

  • •

    MSB and signed predicates reduce to unsigned comparisons after fixed public shifts, and the corresponding masked rewrites follow by applying Lemma 4.3 to the shifted comparisons.

The predicate primitive Πpred\Pi_{\mathrm{pred}} is constructed to output XOR-shares of all masked comparison atoms used in these rewrites (including comparisons against secret mask-derived thresholds such as rinr_{\mathrm{in}} and rinmod2fr_{\mathrm{in}}\bmod 2^{f}). Carry bits (which are constants independent of xx) are provided as XOR-shared constants in preprocessing. Therefore, parties can locally compute XOR-shares of every primitive predicate value on xx.

Step 3: Eliminating Piecewise Boolean Control Flow.

If the Boolean outputs of the operator specification are piecewise, Lemma D.2 rewrites them into a single global Boolean circuit using interval indicators Ji​(x)J_{i}(x). Each Ji​(x)J_{i}(x) is itself a Boolean circuit over comparisons of the form 𝕀[x<αi]\mathbb{I}_{\left[x<\alpha_{i}\right]}, hence can be computed correctly from the masked comparison atoms obtained in Step 2. Consequently, the normalized Boolean circuit evaluates to exactly the Boolean outputs of the operator specification, without revealing the active interval.

Step 4: Correct Arithmetic Outputs via Horner Evaluation.

Parties compute additive shares of x=x^−rinx=\hat{x}-r_{\mathrm{in}} locally (Protocol 2). They hold additive shares of the correct coefficient vector for the active interval from Step 1. Evaluating each polynomial Pi⋆,j​(x)P_{i^{\star},j}(x) of degree at most dd by Horner’s rule uses at most dd ring multiplications (exactly dd if coefficients are padded to degree dd and evaluated uniformly) and yields additive shares of Pi⋆,j​(x)P_{i^{\star},j}(x) by standard Beaver multiplication correctness. This produces additive shares of the arithmetic outputs Pi⋆​(x)P_{i^{\star}}(x).

Step 5: Complexity Bound and “At Most Two” Primitive Evaluations.

The protocol invokes at most one predicate primitive evaluation (Step 2) and at most one lookup primitive evaluation (Step 1), hence at most two non-interactive backend interface evaluations on the same public input x^\hat{x}. Either call can be omitted in degenerate cases (no Boolean outputs/predicates or no interval-dependent coefficients). Horner evaluation uses r⋅dr\cdot d ring multiplications, hence O⁡(r⋅d)O(r\cdot d) Beaver triples. The Boolean circuit cost is captured by its number of AND gates G∧G_{\wedge} and mixed-domain uses GmixG_{\mathrm{mix}}, as stated. ∎

Appendix M A Standard Real/Ideal Security Statement with Explicit Leakage

This section introduces a standard real/ideal statement, including an explicit leakage function. Full proofs are given for the gate-level protocol; end-to-end transformer inference follows by standard composition.

M.1 Leakage Function

For a fixed gate type τ\tau, define the public shape leakage

ℒshape​(τ):=(CLOSE\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{shape}}(\tau):=( T,{kt}t=1T,M,p,\displaystyle T,\{k_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T},M,p,
OPEN#​mults,#​ANDs,#​B2A/A2B),\displaystyle\#\text{mults},\#\text{ANDs},\#\text{B2A/A2B}),

where: TT and {kt}\{k_{t}\} describe the multi-view predicate primitive shape, MM and pp describe the interval lookup shape, and the remaining counts describe how many standard preprocessed subprotocols are invoked in post-processing. By Proposition I.3, this leakage depends only on τ\tau (public).

The online protocol additionally reveals public masked wires such as x^\hat{x} and masked outputs y^\hat{y}; we treat these as explicit leakage:

ℒonline:=(x^, optional masked outputs).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{online}}:=(\hat{x},\text{ optional masked outputs}).

Since x^=x+rin\hat{x}=x+r_{\mathrm{in}} with uniform rinr_{\mathrm{in}}, x^\hat{x} is uniform and information-theoretically independent of xx.

M.2 Ideal Functionality for a Scalar Gate Type (with Leakage)

We define an ideal functionality ℱτℒ\mathcal{F}_{\tau}^{\mathcal{L}} for a gate type τ\tau that captures exactly what the real protocol reveals.

Functionality ℱτℒ\mathcal{F}_{\tau}^{\mathcal{L}} (Informal Description).

On input shares from parties that reconstruct to x∈Rx\in R, the functionality: (i) samples a uniform mask rin←Rr_{\mathrm{in}}\leftarrow R, (ii) outputs x^=x+rinmod2n\hat{x}=x+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bmod 2^{n} to both parties as leakage, (iii) outputs additive/XOR shares of (𝐲,𝐳)=Gτ​(x)(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z})=G_{\tau}(x) to the parties, and (iv) outputs ℒshape​(τ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{shape}}(\tau) as public leakage.

This ideal world models exactly the fact that the protocol reveals masked values but keeps the unmasked xx secret.

M.3 Security of Subprotocols Assumed

We assume standard semi-honest security for:

  • •

    Beaver multiplication over RR,

  • •

    Boolean AND over XOR shares (equivalently, multiplication over ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}),

  • •

    B2A/A2B conversions (when used),

  • •

    and backend primitive families, in the standard “one-key privacy” sense: a single party’s key (and all local evaluations on any polynomial number of inputs) leaks nothing about instance parameters beyond public shape.

These are standard assumptions in the preprocessing MPC literature and in FSS-based secure inference systems.

M.4 Proof of Semi-Honest Security for Compiled Scalar Gates

Theorem M.1 (Gate-level semi-honest security).

Fix a gate type τ\tau and consider the compiled gate protocol for one instance. Under the assumptions in Appendix M.3, for each b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\} there exists a PPT simulator 𝖲𝗂𝗆b\mathsf{Sim}_{b} such that for any input distribution on xx and any auxiliary input, the real view of a semi-honest adversary corrupting PbP_{b} is computationally indistinguishable from the simulator’s output given only:

(\displaystyle( the corrupted party’s input share,its output shares,\displaystyle\text{the corrupted party's input share},\ \text{its output shares},
OPENℒshape​(τ),ℒonline).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{shape}}(\tau),\ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{online}}).

Equivalently, the protocol securely realizes ℱτℒ\mathcal{F}_{\tau}^{\mathcal{L}} in the semi-honest preprocessing model.

Proof.

We construct 𝖲𝗂𝗆b\mathsf{Sim}_{b} by composing simulators for each subprotocol. The simulator is additionally given the corrupted party’s output shares, which are part of the adversary’s view in both the real and ideal executions.

Preprocessing Simulation.

All preprocessing material (masks, backend interface keys, Beaver/AND/B2A correlations) is input-independent. Therefore, 𝖲𝗂𝗆b\mathsf{Sim}_{b} samples the corrupted party’s preprocessing view from the correct distribution conditioned on ℒshape​(τ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{shape}}(\tau) (which fixes public key shapes). This is feasible by the assumed security of backend primitive instances (keys reveal no instance parameters beyond shape) and by standard definitions of preprocessed correlations (Beaver/AND/B2A shares are uniformly random subject to correctness).

Online Simulation: Masked Opening of x^\hat{x}.

In the real protocol, the transcript reveals x^=x+rin\hat{x}=x+r_{\mathrm{in}}, which is uniform over RR. In the ideal world, x^\hat{x} is provided by ℒonline\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{online}}. The simulator programs the shares-to-masked opening messages consistently with this leaked x^\hat{x} (using the fact that the opened value is public and the honest party’s share message is not otherwise constrained). This is the standard simulation for openings of one-time pads.

Online Simulation: Non-Interactive Backend Interface Evaluations.

Backend interface evaluations are local: they produce no interaction transcript. The corrupted party’s internal state includes its local outputs, which are deterministic functions of its key and the public input x^\hat{x}. Since backend interface keys are simulated or sampled to be indistinguishable from real keys of the same shape, the distribution of the corrupted party’s entire local evaluation behavior is indistinguishable.

Online Simulation: Beaver/AND/B2A/A2B Subprotocols.

All interaction beyond revealing masked wires occurs inside standard secure subprotocols: Beaver multiplications open masked differences (e,f)(e,f), Boolean AND opens ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-masked values, and B2A/A2B opens standard masked values. By the assumed semi-honest security of these subprotocols, their transcripts are simulatable given only their public openings and the corrupted party’s local inputs/outputs to those subprotocol calls. Since the overall functionality reveals only masked wires and the protocol does not reveal intermediate unmasked secrets, the simulator can invoke the corresponding subprotocol simulators to generate indistinguishable transcripts.

Composition.

Finally, the protocol is a sequential composition of the above components. Standard composition theorems for semi-honest secure protocols imply that the concatenation of the simulated views is indistinguishable from the real view, completing the proof. ∎

M.5 Security and Correctness for Compiled Gates

Proof Sketch.

Compiled gates instantiate the compiled gate protocol. They then apply a deterministic post-processing map Φτ\Phi_{\tau} using only secure share-based subprotocols. Correctness follows from Theorem 4.6 and the correctness of the post-processing circuit. Security follows from Theorem M.1 and sequential composition. Optional masked outputs satisfy 𝐲^=𝐲+rout\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{y}+r_{\mathrm{out}}. They reveal no information about 𝐲\mathbf{y} since routr_{\mathrm{out}} is fresh uniform. ∎

Appendix N Example: A Complete (F,Φ)(F,\Phi) Pair

This appendix gives a fully concrete specification+post-processing example that can be read independently. The goal is: we pick the smallest operator that (i) has a genuine piecewise structure, (ii) produces at least one predicate bit, and (iii) uses a nontrivial post-processing circuit Φ\Phi. For simplicity we present a signed ReLU gate; real operators (e.g., spline-approximated GELU/SiLU) follow the same pattern with more intervals and higher-degree polynomials.

Target Scalar Gate.

Fix word size nn and let R=ℤ2nR=\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}. Interpret 𝖠n\mathsf{A}_{n} as two’s-complement signed fixed-point with any number of fractional bits; the fractional metadata is irrelevant for this example because the map is homogeneous. Define the scalar gate

GReLU:𝖠n→𝖠n×𝖡,GReLU​(x)=(max⁡(x,0),MSB⁡(x)),G_{\mathrm{ReLU}}:\mathsf{A}_{n}\to\mathsf{A}_{n}\times\mathsf{B},\qquad G_{\mathrm{ReLU}}(x)=\bigl(\max(x,0),\mathrm{MSB}(x)\bigr),

where MSB⁡(x)=1\mathrm{MSB}(x)=1 iff xx is negative in two’s complement.

Operator Specification FcoeffF_{\mathrm{coeff}}.

Instead of directly outputting max⁡(x,0)\max(x,0) as a polynomial piece, we show how to use Φ\Phi by having the operator specification output coefficients for an affine form. Let N=2nN=2^{n} and use the canonical representative rep⁡(x)∈{0,…,N−1}\mathrm{rep}(x)\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}. Consider the partition

0=α0<α1<α2=N,α1=N/2,0=\alpha_{0}<\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}=N,\qquad\alpha_{1}=N/2,

which corresponds to non-negative vs. negative signed values. Thus I0=[0,N/2)I_{0}=[0,N/2) are non-negative representatives and I1=[N/2,N)I_{1}=[N/2,N) are negative representatives.

We define an operator specification

Fcoeff:𝖠n→𝖠n2×𝖡F_{\mathrm{coeff}}:\mathsf{A}_{n}\to\mathsf{A}_{n}^{2}\times\mathsf{B}

with r=2r=2 arithmetic outputs, the affine coefficients a,b∈Ra,b\in R and ℓ=1\ell=1 Boolean output (the sign bit zz). All arithmetic pieces are degree-00 polynomials:

P0​(x)=(a,b)=(1,0),P1​(x)=(a,b)=(0,0).P_{0}(x)=(a,b)=(1,0),\qquad P_{1}(x)=(a,b)=(0,0).

For the Boolean output we use the primitive predicate MSB⁡(x)\mathrm{MSB}(x):

B0​(x)=B1​(x)=MSB⁡(x).B_{0}(x)=B_{1}(x)=\mathrm{MSB}(x).

In words: Fcoeff​(x)F_{\mathrm{coeff}}(x) returns the pair (a,b)(a,b) such that a⋅x+b=max⁡(x,0)a\cdot x+b=\max(x,0), together with z=MSB⁡(x)z=\mathrm{MSB}(x).

Post-Processing Circuit ΦReLU\Phi_{\mathrm{ReLU}}.

Let ΦReLU\Phi_{\mathrm{ReLU}} take as input: (i) additive shares of (a,b)(a,b) from Fcoeff​(x)F_{\mathrm{coeff}}(x), (ii) an XOR-sharing ⟨z⟩\langle z\rangle of z=MSB⁡(x)z=\mathrm{MSB}(x), (iii) additive shares of xx (derived from a public masked opening), and return (y,z)(y,z) where

y=a⋅x+b∈R.y=a\cdot x+b\in R.

Concretely, ΦReLU\Phi_{\mathrm{ReLU}} uses one Beaver multiplication for a⋅xa\cdot x and then local addition of bb. The Boolean output zz is simply forwarded.

Compiled to Two Backend Calls.

Let preprocessing sample a uniform mask rin∈Rr_{\mathrm{in}}\in R and distribute ⟦rin⟧\llbracket r_{\mathrm{in}}\rrbracket. Online evaluation will open the public masked value x^=x+rinmodN\hat{x}=x+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bmod N using Protocol 1.

Interval lookup instance Πcoeff\Pi_{\mathrm{coeff}}. There are m=2m=2 original intervals, so we allocate M=min⁡(m+1,N)=3M=\min(m+1,N)=3 intervals after padding (Protocol 3). The translated starts are

s0=(α0+rin)modN=rin,s1=(α1+rin)modN=(rin+N/2)modN.s_{0}=(\alpha_{0}+r_{\mathrm{in}})\bmod N=r_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad s_{1}=(\alpha_{1}+r_{\mathrm{in}})\bmod N=(r_{\mathrm{in}}+N/2)\bmod N.

Sorting {s0,s1}\{s_{0},s_{1}\} yields (β0,β1)(\beta_{0},\beta_{1}) and an order vector π\pi. Following Protocol 3, we construct boundaries B=(B0,…,BM)B=(B_{0},\ldots,B_{M}) and an index list ord∈{0,1}M\mathrm{ord}\in\{0,1\}^{M} that may duplicate one payload so that the public lookup shape (M,p)(M,p) is independent of the sampled mask. The payload dimension is p=2p=2 and each payload is

vj=(aordj,bordj)∈R2.v_{j}=(a_{\mathrm{ord}_{j}},b_{\mathrm{ord}_{j}})\in R^{2}.

Evaluating Πcoeff\Pi_{\mathrm{coeff}} on the public x^\hat{x} returns additive shares of the correct (a,b)(a,b) without revealing the active interval.

Packed-comparison instance Πpred\Pi_{\mathrm{pred}}. To compute z=MSB⁡(x)z=\mathrm{MSB}(x), we can use MSB​(x)=¬CN/2​(x)\mathrm{MSB}(x)=\neg C_{N/2}(x), where Cβ(x)=𝕀[x<β]C_{\beta}(x)=\mathbb{I}_{\left[x<\beta\right]}. Applying Lemma 4.3 with β=N/2\beta=N/2 yields

CN/2(x)=𝕀[x^<θ]⊕𝕀[x^<rin]⊕w,θ=(rin+N/2)modN,C_{N/2}(x)=\mathbb{I}_{\left[\hat{x}<\theta\right]}\;\oplus\;\mathbb{I}_{\left[\hat{x}<r_{\mathrm{in}}\right]}\;\oplus\;w,\qquad\theta=(r_{\mathrm{in}}+N/2)\bmod N,

where w=𝕀[rin+N/2≥N]w=\mathbb{I}_{\left[r_{\mathrm{in}}+N/2\geq N\right]} is a carry bit that depends only on the mask and is therefore provided as a secret-shared preprocessing constant. Thus the packed-comparison query list contains the two atoms 𝕀[x^<θ]\mathbb{I}_{\left[\hat{x}<\theta\right]} and 𝕀[x^<rin]\mathbb{I}_{\left[\hat{x}<r_{\mathrm{in}}\right]} (both width k=nk=n). Parties locally combine these XOR-shared atoms with ⟨w⟩\langle w\rangle to obtain ⟨CN/2​(x)⟩\langle C_{N/2}(x)\rangle, and then locally negate to get ⟨z⟩=⟨MSB⁡(x)⟩\langle z\rangle=\langle\mathrm{MSB}(x)\rangle.

End-to-End Online Evaluation.

Given an input ⟦x⟧\llbracket x\rrbracket, parties: (i) open x^=x+rin\hat{x}=x+r_{\mathrm{in}} (Protocol 1); (ii) locally evaluate the two backend instances on x^\hat{x} to obtain ⟨z⟩\langle z\rangle and ⟦(a,b)⟧\llbracket(a,b)\rrbracket; (iii) locally derive ⟦x⟧\llbracket x\rrbracket from x^\hat{x} and ⟦rin⟧\llbracket r_{\mathrm{in}}\rrbracket (Protocol 2); (iv) run ΦReLU\Phi_{\mathrm{ReLU}} to compute ⟦y⟧=a⋅x+b\llbracket y\rrbracket=a\cdot x+b and output (⟦y⟧,⟨z⟩)(\llbracket y\rrbracket,\langle z\rangle).

Remark: Extending to a Small GELU Example.

To specify a spline-approximated GELU, one would keep the same structure but set r=1r=1 and choose m>2m>2 intervals with degree-dd polynomials Pi​(x)P_{i}(x). Then Πcoeff\Pi_{\mathrm{coeff}} returns the active interval’s coefficient vector and the post-processing runs Horner evaluation (Theorem 4.6).

Appendix O Complexity Accounting for a Compiled Gate

Let TT be the emitted number of primitive masked comparison atoms in Πpred\Pi_{\mathrm{pred}} after any specification-only syntactic deduplication and optional padding, so that TT depends only on the public operator specification and metadata. Let MM and pp be the interval count and payload dimension of Πcoeff\Pi_{\mathrm{coeff}} under the padding convention, where M:=min⁡(m+1,2n)M:=\min(m+1,2^{n}) for an operator specification with mm original intervals (Proposition I.3). Let MAM_{\mathrm{A}} be the number of ring multiplications (implemented via Beaver triples) performed in post-processing (Horner evaluation plus any extra multiplications in Φ\Phi; cf. Theorem 4.6), let MBM_{\mathrm{B}} be the number of Boolean ANDs, and let GmixG_{\mathrm{mix}} be the number of mixed-domain conversions.

A compiled gate instance uses:

  • •

    One packed-comparison primitive instance with output length TT (or omitted if T=0T=0),

  • •

    One interval-lookup primitive instance with (M,p)(M,p) (or omitted if the arithmetic payload is interval-independent, e.g., the operator specification has a single interval),

  • •

    MAM_{\mathrm{A}} Beaver multiplications over RR,

  • •

    MBM_{\mathrm{B}} preprocessed Boolean ANDs over ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2},

  • •

    GmixG_{\mathrm{mix}} mixed-domain conversions (B2A/A2B).

This accounting is backend-agnostic: concrete preprocessing size/time follows by instantiating the primitive and preprocessing costs of the chosen backend interface and triple-generation mechanisms.
